title: Trump Orders Iran Operation Hours After Criticizing Nuclear Talks
description_short: Trump said he was unhappy with Iran nuclear talks; about three hours later, he ordered Operation Epic Fury, AP reports.
description_medium: The Associated Press reported that on February 27, 2026, President Donald Trump told reporters he was unhappy with the progress of nuclear talks with Iran. About three hours later, while aboard Air Force One, he ordered Operation Epic Fury. AP’s timeline documents the sequence; it does not establish a public set of criteria that changed or show that urgency rhetoric outweighed such criteria.
description_long: The Associated Press reconstructed the hours before the U.S. operation against Iran on February 27, 2026. At the White House, Trump told reporters that he was not pleased with how nuclear talks with Iran were going. Later, at 3:38 p.m. Eastern while aboard Air Force One, he gave the order to launch Operation Epic Fury, according to the timeline AP attributed to military briefings and reporting. At 4:03 p.m., after landing in Texas, Trump again discussed negotiations with reporters. AP reported that the operation killed Iran’s supreme leader, Ali Khamenei, and senior military officials. This chronology supports an account of Trump’s stated dissatisfaction and the timing of his order. It does not establish that he had announced stable public criteria for military action, that those criteria shifted, or that urgency language “outweighed” them. Those broader claims should be removed unless separately documented. The supplied AP URL is the exact story on which this narrower account is based.
notes: The supplied AP URL resolves to AP’s March 2, 2026 timeline. It reports Trump’s dissatisfaction with the Iran nuclear talks at the White House and his order roughly three hours later aboard Air Force One. No evidence in that report supports the original comparison to stable public criteria or an ongoing urgency narrative.
proposed_correction: AP documents Trump’s stated dissatisfaction with Iran nuclear talks and his order for Operation Epic Fury roughly three hours later on February 27, 2026. It does not support a claim that stable public criteria were overridden.

sources.what_it_supports: AP timeline of Trump’s comments on Iran nuclear talks and the Operation Epic Fury order on February 27, 2026.

supported_facts: AP published a timeline dated March 2, 2026, based on events of February 27.
Trump told reporters at the White House he was unhappy with the progress of nuclear talks.
At 3:38 p.m. Eastern, aboard Air Force One, Trump ordered Operation Epic Fury, according to AP’s timeline.
AP reports that the operation killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei and senior military officials.
limitations: The article documents chronology and attributed statements, not Trump’s private motive.
It does not identify stable public decision criteria or demonstrate that urgency language outweighed them.
evidence_resolution.proposed_title: Trump Orders Iran Operation Hours After Criticizing Nuclear Talks
evidence_resolution.proposed_claim: AP documents Trump’s stated dissatisfaction with Iran nuclear talks and his order for Operation Epic Fury roughly three hours later on February 27, 2026. It does not support a claim that stable public criteria were overridden.

title: Nida Allam Concedes to Valerie Foushee in North Carolina’s 4th District Primary
description_short: Progressive challenger Nida Allam conceded to Rep. Valerie Foushee in the 2026 Democratic primary for North Carolina’s 4th District.
description_medium: NPR and North Carolina Public Radio reported that Durham County Commissioner Nida Allam conceded to incumbent Rep. Valerie Foushee in the March 2026 Democratic primary for North Carolina’s 4th Congressional District. Allam conceded while ballots were still being counted, and AP had not yet called the race at that point. NPR described the contest as a test of appetite for generational change among Democrats and reported that Allam campaigned against President Trump’s agenda.
description_long: Nida Allam, a Durham County commissioner and progressive challenger, conceded to Democratic Rep. Valerie Foushee in the March 3, 2026 primary for North Carolina’s 4th Congressional District. NPR reported the concession on March 4, while ballots were still being counted. North Carolina Public Radio reported that the Associated Press had not formally called the race at the time and that election officials were preparing to process provisional ballots. The race was viewed as an early test of Democratic voters’ appetite for generational change. NPR described Allam’s campaign as further to Foushee’s left and said Allam presented herself as a stronger opponent of President Donald Trump’s agenda. Those are reported political positions and context, not evidence that Trump intervened in the primary or that the election was manipulated. Subsequent election results showed Foushee winning the primary. The supplied New York Times article page was inaccessible in the earlier source check, but NPR and WUNC provide the candidate names, district, concession, and contemporaneous vote-count status. The entry should describe the primary and concession, not classify the event as election interference.

proposed_correction: Nida Allam conceded to Valerie Foushee in the 2026 Democratic primary for North Carolina’s 4th District; Allam’s campaign positioned her as a stronger opponent of Trump’s agenda.

title: Donald and Ivana Trump Married in 1977 After Signing a Prenuptial Agreement
description_short: Donald and Ivana Trump married in 1977; a 1990 report says they had worked out a prenuptial agreement before the wedding.
description_medium: The New York Times reported in February 1990 that Donald and Ivana Trump had worked out a prenuptial agreement before their 1977 wedding. A New York appellate decision later records that they married on April 9, 1977, and identifies later postnuptial agreements. These sources support the marriage and existence of a premarital agreement, but not the claim that it required them to have three children.
description_long: Donald and Ivana Trump married in 1977. In its February 15, 1990 report on their divorce dispute, The New York Times described a prenuptial agreement the couple had worked out before the wedding, along with three later postnuptial agreements. A New York appellate decision in Trump v. Trump states that they married on April 9, 1977, and discusses a 1987 postnuptial agreement and earlier agreements. Together, these sources support a concise account of the marriage and the existence of premarital financial arrangements. They do not establish that the prenuptial agreement required the couple to have three children, nor do they substantiate the “bizarre deal” framing in the original title. The supplied TrumpFile page makes claims about particular contract terms, but the underlying agreement was not produced in the source packet and the linked New York Times article discusses the divorce litigation rather than confirming those specific terms. The entry should therefore retain the documented marriage and agreement history and omit the alleged child requirement and any unverified payment promise.
organization_tags: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division

preserved_fields.description_short: Donald Trump marries Ivana in bizarre deal, required to have three children

proposed_correction: Donald and Ivana Trump married on April 9, 1977, after working out a prenuptial agreement; the alleged three-child clause is unverified.

title: Project 2025 Tax Proposals Could Affect the Child Tax Credit and EITC
description_short: Project 2025’s tax proposal does not specify whether the Child Tax Credit or EITC would be cut; cited tax effects are conditional projections.
description_medium: A 2024 Joint Economic Committee analysis says Project 2025 proposed removing “most deductions, credits, and exclusions,” but did not specify whether the Child Tax Credit or Earned Income Tax Credit would remain. It estimates that a $90,000 family of four could pay about $6,300 more if the Child Tax Credit were also eliminated. The National Association of Social Workers says eliminating the EITC could affect 23 million taxpayers. These are projections about a proposal, not enacted cuts.
description_long: The Joint Economic Committee’s August 2024 analysis of Project 2025 said the plan proposed removing “most deductions, credits, and exclusions” but did not specify whether the Child Tax Credit (CTC) or Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC) would be retained. The committee estimated that a family of four earning $90,000 would have paid roughly $2,300 more under the plan’s proposed tax rates in its model; if the CTC were also eliminated, the estimated increase would be about $6,300. The National Association of Social Workers summarized the proposal as unspecified about which credits would be removed and said eliminating the EITC could leave 23 million taxpayers without that source of income and push people further into poverty. These figures describe conditional scenarios and an advocacy group’s account of projected effects. They do not show that Trump eliminated either credit, that the proposed cuts were enacted, or that a $120 billion program termination occurred. The entry should therefore be framed as a proposed tax-policy risk with assumptions attached. Any description of actual benefit loss requires enacted statutory or administrative evidence identifying a change, its effective date, and the people affected.
notes: JEC and NASW describe proposals and conditional modeled impacts. The JEC’s $6,300 estimate assumes CTC elimination; the sources do not document enacted termination of either credit.
proposed_correction: Project 2025’s proposal to remove most tax deductions, credits, and exclusions left CTC/EITC treatment unspecified; cited effects are conditional estimates, not enacted cuts.

sources.what_it_supports: JEC analysis of Project 2025 tax proposals and conditional family tax estimates.
NASW brief discussing unspecified tax-credit changes and projected EITC effects.

supported_facts: The JEC analysis is dated August 1, 2024 and describes proposed tax changes in Project 2025.
The plan’s “most deductions, credits, and exclusions” language does not specify whether CTC or EITC would remain.
JEC estimates roughly $6,300 additional tax for a $90,000 family of four only if the CTC were also eliminated.
NASW reports that eliminating the EITC could affect 23 million taxpayers.
limitations: No cited source establishes that either credit was repealed or that Trump implemented such a termination.
Figures are conditional projections; the $120 billion amount in the old title is not substantiated by these sources.
evidence_resolution.proposed_title: Project 2025 Tax Proposals Could Affect the Child Tax Credit and EITC
evidence_resolution.proposed_claim: Project 2025’s proposal to remove most tax deductions, credits, and exclusions left CTC/EITC treatment unspecified; cited effects are conditional estimates, not enacted cuts.

title: Dan Coats Resigns as DNI After Public Disagreements With Trump
description_short: Dan Coats resigned as director of national intelligence in 2019 after public disagreements with Trump over Russia; Trump announced a replacement.
description_medium: The Office of the Director of National Intelligence published Dan Coats’s resignation letter on July 28, 2019, saying it would take effect August 15. The Associated Press reported that Coats and Trump had often been at odds over Russian interference in the 2016 election, including after Trump publicly doubted the intelligence assessment at Helsinki. The record supports a resignation amid public disagreements, not a firing for refusing to alter findings.
description_long: Daniel Coats resigned as director of national intelligence in July 2019. The Office of the Director of National Intelligence published his letter on July 28 and stated that his resignation would become effective August 15. The Associated Press reported that Coats and President Donald Trump had often been at odds over Russian interference in the 2016 election. It described a public disagreement after Trump’s 2018 Helsinki news conference with Vladimir Putin, when Trump said he saw no reason to believe Russia interfered and Coats publicly reaffirmed the intelligence community’s assessment of Russian interference and ongoing efforts. Separately, 2017 reporting by NPR, citing unnamed current and former officials, said Trump asked Coats and the NSA director to push back against the FBI Russia investigation; the report said both declined. These reports do not show that Trump fired Coats or that the 2019 resignation was caused by a refusal to manipulate intelligence. The title should distinguish the documented resignation and public disagreements from the earlier, anonymously sourced account of requests to influence public messaging. The official resignation letter confirms the departure and its effective date, not its motive.
organization_tags: Office of the Director of National Intelligence

preserved_fields.title: Trump fires Intel Director after he refuses to manipulate Russia findings
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump fires Intel Director after he refuses to manipulate Russia findings

notes: ODNI’s published letter confirms Coats resigned and gives the effective date. AP documents public disagreements over the Russia assessment. NPR’s 2017 report about requests to push back relied on anonymous officials and does not establish that Coats was fired in 2019.
proposed_correction: Coats resigned as DNI in 2019 after documented public disagreements with Trump over Russia; a separate 2017 report described requests to push back against the FBI Russia probe.

limitations: The official letter does not state why Coats resigned.
The evidence does not support saying Trump fired Coats or that the 2019 resignation directly followed a specific refusal to alter findings.
evidence_resolution.proposed_title: Dan Coats Resigns as DNI After Public Disagreements With Trump
evidence_resolution.proposed_claim: Coats resigned as DNI in 2019 after documented public disagreements with Trump over Russia; a separate 2017 report described requests to push back against the FBI Russia probe.

title: Trump Allies Circulate a 2025 Draft Order Proposing Federal Election Controls
description_short: A draft order dated April 12, 2025, proposed emergency powers over election administration; reporting says Trump had not adopted it.
description_medium: Democracy Docket reported that Peter Ticktin, a Trump ally, provided a draft executive order dated April 12, 2025, that proposed declaring a national emergency and expanding federal control over voting. The published draft proposes measures including hand-marked and hand-counted ballots and limits on mail voting. The Washington Post reported on an earlier version, and PBS later reported Trump said he was not considering the draft. It was a proposal, not an enacted order.
description_long: In February 2026, Democracy Docket published a 17-page draft executive order dated April 12, 2025, titled “Establishing Security, Integrity, and Transparency for United States Elections with Protections Against Foreign Interference.” Peter Ticktin, a Trump ally involved in the effort, provided that version to the outlet. The draft proposed invoking a national emergency and granting federal agencies roles in election administration. Its text included proposals for hand-marked and hand-counted paper ballots, new voter registration with proof of citizenship for the 2026 midterms, and limits on mail voting. The Washington Post reported that activists were circulating an earlier version and that a version it reviewed cited alleged Chinese interference in the 2020 election. Democracy Docket reported that the version Ticktin provided did not include that China claim. These are provisions in a proposed document, not implemented policy. PBS reported that Trump said he was not considering an emergency declaration for the midterms, and the reporting does not establish that Trump authored or approved the draft. The item should describe the document’s circulation and proposed provisions while keeping the authorship and White House coordination claims attributed.

preserved_fields.title: Trump allies draft executive order to take control over elections
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump allies draft executive order to take control over elections

notes: Democracy Docket published and linked the April 12, 2025 draft; its reporting identifies Ticktin as the provider, not necessarily the author. The Washington Post describes an earlier version. PBS reports Trump said he was not considering the proposal. No evidence shows enactment.
proposed_correction: Trump allies circulated a draft dated April 12, 2025 proposing emergency federal control over aspects of voting; it was not an enacted order, and authorship/White House coordination remain attributed claims.

Reporting that Trump said he was not considering the draft proposal.

limitations: Ticktin’s role in providing a version does not prove he wrote the full document.
The draft was not an enacted executive order; the evidence does not establish Trump’s approval or implementation.
The Washington Post’s earlier draft reportedly differed from the version published by Democracy Docket.
